Dear Representative Nadler,

How absolutely mortifying to watch the former Chairman of the House Judiciary Committee demonstrate such spectacular constitutional ignorance. Your decades in Congress and your leadership role overseeing constitutional matters makes this legal malpractice even more embarrassing than your fourteen colleagues who've already humiliated themselves today.

Let me help clarify what actually happened here, since constitutional law apparently wasn't retained during your tenure as Judiciary Chairman. The Supreme Court didn't rule that patients "cannot sue to see their qualified provider" – they clarified that states have Tenth Amendment authority to decide how to spend their Medicaid dollars. You know, that pesky concept called federalism that you should understand better than almost anyone in Congress given your committee leadership.

Your claim that "Congress guaranteed that right nearly 60 years ago" is constitutionally illiterate. Congress has no enumerated power to guarantee healthcare provider choice – that authority belongs to states under the Tenth Amendment. As former Judiciary Chairman, you should know that federal overreach doesn't become constitutional just because Congress passes a law claiming authority it doesn't possess.

Your "attack on reproductive freedom" hysteria is particularly rich when basic reproductive responsibility costs about $1 per condom (or as little as 33 cents each when you buy a 12-pack). We're talking about approximately $12 per year for comprehensive birth control – less than you probably spend on a single New York deli sandwich. Are you seriously suggesting Americans can't afford $12 annually for personal responsibility, or are you just so committed to government dependency that you can't imagine people managing their own healthcare without federal bureaucrats?

Here's what's really shameful about your constitutional confusion: you're demanding taxpayer funding for one specific organization while completely ignoring that organizations like PreBorn! operate entirely without government subsidies, providing free ultrasounds, counseling, and comprehensive support to women nationwide. There are also over 1,400 federally qualified health centers, thousands of community health centers, private practices, and faith-based organizations providing the exact same cancer screenings, STI testing, and wellness exams you claim are threatened. But acknowledging these alternatives would undermine your entire government-dependency narrative.

Your defense of Planned Parenthood is particularly disturbing given your role as a supposed constitutional guardian. You're championing an organization founded by Margaret Sanger specifically to control population growth in minority communities. The same Democratic Party that defended slavery, created Jim Crow laws, and founded Planned Parenthood to (in Sanger's own words) manage "undesirable" populations now claims to champion healthcare freedom. Your entire platform is built on keeping minorities dependent on government programs instead of empowering them with economic freedom – it's the same plantation system with civil rights rhetoric.

Speaking of congressional guarantees, remember when your party guaranteed the Affordable Care Act would ensure "healthcare for all Americans"? Obama promised universal coverage, that premiums would go down by $2,500, and that "if you like your healthcare plan, you can keep it." Instead, up to 9.3 million people lost their coverage, premiums increased by 60% in the first four years, and PolitiFact named Obama's promise the "Lie of the Year." Your party guaranteed universal healthcare coverage through the ACA – so why are you still demanding special funding for one organization when you supposedly already achieved comprehensive coverage?

Your constitutional ignorance is particularly shameful for someone who chaired the House Judiciary Committee. The federal government has zero enumerated power to fund healthcare organizations or guarantee provider choice. That authority belongs to states under the Tenth Amendment. So your outrage about this decision is actually directed at the Court for... upholding the Constitution you spent years supposedly defending as Judiciary Chairman. Your constitutional malpractice is a disgrace to your former position.

Your claim about "dismantling Planned Parenthood from the bench" is both factually false and legally ignorant. The Court didn't dismantle anything – they upheld constitutional federalism. Healthcare services are available at thousands of locations nationwide beyond one politically-connected abortion provider. You know this, but spreading constitutional confusion helps your fundraising and keeps your progressive base mobilized.

Perhaps between your constitutional malpractice and your committee leadership failures, you could explain why taxpayers should fund your preferred political organization when thousands of other healthcare providers exist? Or why we need special funding for one organization when your party guaranteed universal healthcare coverage? Or why you're violating your oath to defend the Constitution? Or why you can't formulate an original thought instead of copying fourteen other Democrats who already embarrassed themselves with identical talking points?

But what do I know? I'm just someone who actually studied constitutional law and retained the information, unlike someone who apparently used their Judiciary Committee chairmanship to advance partisan politics while ignoring the constitutional principles they were supposed to protect. Your constitutional ignorance is a disgrace to your former position and an embarrassment to institutional governance.

Effects on Medicaid
Spending Reductions: The bill reduces federal Medicaid spending by $700–$880 billion over 10 years, representing a 12% cut in projected spending. This includes reducing the federal share of Medicaid payments in some states (e.g., from 90% to 80% in certain cases), with state-specific cuts ranging from 5% (Wyoming, Alabama) to 17% (Washington).

Enrollment Impact: An estimated 8.6–10.3 million people could lose Medicaid coverage by 2034 due to work requirements, more frequent eligibility checks (every six months), and co-payments for expansion enrollees. States like Washington and Virginia may see enrollment drop by 26% and 21%, respectively.

Program Changes: The bill introduces work and reporting requirements, described by Republicans as targeting "waste, fraud, and abuse," though critics argue these measures disproportionately affect vulnerable populations, including 190,000 people in Louisiana alone. Co-payments and paperwork burdens may deter low-income individuals from accessing care.

Long-Term Care Concerns: Cuts could strain long-term care for older adults, particularly in nursing homes, as Medicaid is a primary payer for such services. Reduced funding may lead to staffing shortages and lower-quality care, especially for poorer seniors.
